title: The tree in winter
hookLine: a bare tree in winter, and an eighteen-year-old who sees the spring that isn't there yet
tomorrow: before the monastery, what kind of servant was he?

lines: A TREE WITH NOTHING ON IT.
cards: Nobody posts the winter view. Gray sky, slush by the curb, trees that look like wire. It's the season most feeds skip.
Long before Thérèse, a young man in France stops in front of a tree like that. It's winter. The tree has nothing on it, not one leaf.
He's eighteen. Nothing about this tree is beautiful, and nothing about the moment looks important. But something happens while he stands there, and he'll still be talking about it as an old man.

teach.b: This is Brother Lawrence, who became a lay brother in a Carmelite monastery. The book with his name on it, The Practice of the Presence of God, isn't one he sat down to write.
It's mostly a visitor's notes of conversations with him, plus some of his letters. And the first conversation opens with the tree.
Lawrence told his visitor that God did him a singular favor in his conversion, at eighteen.
It was winter, and he saw a tree stripped of its leaves.
He considered that in a little while the leaves would come back, and after them the flowers, and then the fruit. Nothing on the branch proved it.
From that sight, he said, he received a high view of the providence and power of God that never left his soul.
It set him loose from the world, and lit a love for God so strong that, more than forty years on, he couldn't tell whether it had grown since. Notice what he didn't get.
Just a bare thing, looked at with hope. That's the whole book in small: God found in plain things, ordinary days, kitchens and errands.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: a spiritual classic starts with a man staring at a tree with no leaves.

how: Catholics who read Brother Lawrence often take a few pages at a time, and some come back to the winter tree when a season of life feels bare.

games.q: what does “the tree in winter” mean?
o: a carol about a tree sung at Christmas Mass
a tree Lawrence planted in the monastery garden
a bare winter tree that showed Lawrence spring was coming

games.q: the tree in winter — tap the pairs.
p: a high view of God's providence

s: Brother Lawrence wrote The Practice of the Presence of God as a book
it's mostly a visitor's notes of conversations with him, plus some of his letters.
his turning point came from looking at a bare winter tree
leaves, then flowers, then fruit, all still to come.
Lawrence's conversion came through a vision
no voice, no vision: a bare tree, looked at with hope.

games.q: your neighbor lost his job in the middle of winter. he says nothing's happening and nothing's coming. what does Lawrence's tree say?
o: a bare season isn't a dead one; what's coming may not show yet.
cheer up, because everything happens for a reason.
he's right to expect nothing; winter means it's over.
games.why: Lawrence saw no leaves at all and still saw spring coming, and with it God's providence. hope without proof on the branch.

practice: If there's a window near you, find a tree and look at its branches; if not, bring one to mind, or look at any plant in the room. Rest your eyes on the bare parts, the places where nothing is happening yet.
Keep looking while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: The tree in winter. A bare tree that showed a young man the spring he couldn't see yet.

orig.note: his name in religion, in French: Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection.

carryVoice: Your line: spring will come. A bare branch isn't the same as a dead one. See you tomorrow.
